utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. McElligott.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I remind you that you are still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. McElligott. I'm Defence counsel for Mr. Martic, the accused, and my name is Predrag Milovancevic and I will now start your cross examination. Although we speak different languages, I kindly ask you to make sure nonetheless to make a small pause before answering my questions so that the interpreters can do their job properly. Thank you. Your statement to the OTP, given in November 2004, can be found in e-court, and I believe there is no need for copies to be handed out to those present in the courtroom. From your personal background, I can see that you were born in 1945, in Ireland, and that upon completing secondary education in 1964, you joined the Irish police force, from which you were retired in 2001. I'd like to know which high school you completed.

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I completed the secondary school level, that is the level I got to, at the age of 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you proceed, Mr. Milovancevic, where in e-court can we find the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I should have done that beforehand. 1D0047 is the reference number.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. The witness, I believe, doesn't have a copy of the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's visible here.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: I'm told it's visible on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I also have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Having completed -- or, rather, having joined the Irish police force in 1964, you were promoted to the position of detective superintendent, if I remember well, from your examination-in-chief. I'd like to know whether, upon completing secondary education and after having joined the police force, you attended any other schools?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I did a management course with the Irish management institute. It would be perhaps a first level management course around the time I was promoted to sergeant. I also did a subsequent management course with the open university, and our police college also ran training courses for the rank of inspector and superintendent, so I undertook all those courses as I progressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. These details cannot be found in your statement. That is why I put these questions to you. You state in paragraph 4 of your statement that on two separate occasions you served with the United Nations; the first time was in 1988-1989 where you were head of communications with the United Nations mission in Namibia, and then in 1992-1993, you served with UNPROFOR in the former Yugoslavia. Now, in connection with the fact that you served on two missions with the UN, I'd like to know the following: Whether the main principle governing any UN mission is objectivity and impartiality of the United Nations staff?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Between 2nd October, 1992, and 2nd October, 1993, you were serving with the civilian police of the United Nations headquartered in -- at the UNPROFOR head office in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should be up to the 1st of November, 1993, Your Honours. Statement does show the 2nd of October, but on reflection I'm satisfied it was the 1st of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 6, you also explained that the peacekeeping mission of the United Nations based on the Vance Plan concept, led to the deployment of troops and monitors of the United Nations, police monitors to certain areas designated as United Nations Protected Areas, UNPAs. I'd like to know whether these protected areas, that is the UNPA areas were identical to the areas covered by the United Nations civilian police.

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The UNPAs were the United Nations protected areas and then pink zones extended further territory on to what was known as the UN -- United Nations Protected Areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I put this question in reference to your explanation that is contained in paragraphs 14 through 17 in your statement where you state that the sectors of the civilian police of the United Nations were Sector North, Sector South, Sector East and Sector West, with the corresponding head seats, and I merely wanted to know whether your areas of responsibility corresponded to the UNPA zones, but I believe that with your earlier answer, you've already answered my question. Witness, you heard my question. Did you -- is that the answer that you gave earlier on? Was that an answer to this question of mine? That's what I was asking you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood to you say that you had got the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed, thank you. You had said that he had answered you previously, Mr. Milovancevic, so in fact the position is you shouldn't have asked the question the second time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 6, where you speak of the UNPAs, you state that these were the areas that should have been demilitarised and that the role of the UN troops was to ensure that the area remained demilitarised and that all persons in them would be protected from fear and armed attack, and that any such attacks were to be prevented. Can you tell me that in the period when you served with the UNCIVPOL, whether the UNPROFOR fulfilled its mission and prevented the UNPAs from any attacks?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Protected the UNPAs from any attack.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The mission, Your Honour, was most difficult, and I think the first difficult step arose when the policing element of it came into being. The Vance Plan provided for the local police to be the police force in the area and that they would carry side-arms. Now, I understand that up to 16.000 other people were put into uniform and armed to a different level completely, long arms and a variety of weaponry was available to these people, and that did not help the UN mission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do I recollect your evidence-in-chief correctly that the UN civil police were not armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unarmed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And do I also recollect your evidence-in-chief correctly that maintenance of law and order was the responsibility of the local police and not the civil police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Defence counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. McElligott, in answering my previous question, you spoke of the difficulties that the UN mission was faced with, but you didn't answer my question, which was whether during your term of office there, were there any acts of aggression or attacks on these UNPAs from the outside areas or not? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There were. There were incursions and I would -- fair to say there were incursions on all sides, and I remember specifically if he is probing, that there were incursions from the Croatian side, and I recall one in particular at Benkovac in January and I think the Medak pocket is another one of note. So there were, there were serious attacks, and indeed there were random attacks on individuals from time to time. I suppose local conflicts broke out somewhere along the border areas and individuals were killed. I have a specific recollection of a protest coming from the Croatian authorities in relation to an attack on their people at a certain time, and I did a survey of it and at that time I found that the Croatian authorities had actually killed more people than the Serbs did in that particular area over a specific time. So it was very much -- you know, there were incidents on all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now that you mentioned the Maslenica incident and the Medak pocket incident, do you know that because of the Maslenica action, the Security Council of the United Nations passed the -- passed Resolution 802 whereby the Croatian forces were asked to withdraw from the area; and do you know -- are you aware of the fact that during the operation, 491 persons were killed, eight went missing, at least 10 Serb villages in the areas that came under this act of aggression were totally devastated, including properties, homes, churches, and that the local population was expelled? Are you aware of these facts?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this stage I'm not aware of the detail of it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you answer, counsel for the Prosecution is on her feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just -- I'm just going to object to this line of questioning on the ground of relevance. What is the relevance of this line of questioning to the crimes in this indictment, in this case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The relevance of the question should stem from an attempt of the Defence to establish what this witness's understanding of the UN mission and UNPROFOR mission was, what his understanding of the UNCIVPOL mission was and what -- and in what way he approached certain situations arising on the ground. A whole series of documents that were tendered through this witness deal with these matters, and that was the reason why I put the question. The witness himself, in his statement, spoke of the role of the United Nations, and I'd like to know in what way this role was materialised on the ground at the time when he was there, and when he was in charge of the functions that the United Nations assumed upon themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ms. Valabhji? Any reply?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. No reply. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Objection overruled. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: My last question was quite extensive but it had to do with one topic only and that's the Maslenica operation. Can you tell us anything about it, based on the question I put to you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the Resolution 802, Your Honour, I recall drafting a police proposal for the policing of that area subsequent to 802, and as far as I can recall, 802 covered Maslenica, Pocitelj, and I think there was a third village mentioned in 802, if my memory is correct. And I remember drafting a proposal and I under -- my memory is that it did not materialise into a reality, so that that plan that we had I think there was detailed discussions in relation to the policing of the area, and I had a plan prepared to do it but it didn't come to fruition. But the detail of what actually happened there, I don't have that clearly here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, sir. On the issue of the Resolution 802, do you know whether the Croatian side had honoured the decision which is contained in the United Nations Resolution 802, to withdraw from those areas that it had seized in the course of this operation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honour. All I know is that I did prepare the plan and it did not come to fruition, so I'm not sure where the detail of it broke down, recalling something that's perhaps 13 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned another operation that took place in the area you were in charge of, at the time when you were there, which is operation Medak pocket, which became quite notorious for the extreme brutality of the Croatian forces. Are you aware of the victims the Serbian side suffered during this operation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the Medak pocket subsequent to the event and I saw it at firsthand. So I am quite familiar with the devastation that was caused. I suppose it would be fair to say that the area was rendered inhabitable following the attack. Apart from the loss of human life, it would be fair to say that the plan was to make sure that nobody lived there again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As an eye-witness of what transpired at Medak pocket, those were three Serb villages, Citluk, Divoselo and Pocitelj which were completely destroyed. As an eye-witness, would you agree with General Jean Cot words --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt your question? Mr. Milovancevic, was this witness an eye-witness to these events, was he present when they took place incidents took place, or did he go there subsequent to the taking place?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness explained that he went over there after the incident and spoke of the situation as he saw it there. My question was: Based on what he experienced there, would he agree with an assessment of General Jean Cot who had also toured the area at the time and said that this was systematic, deliberate and full destruction. I did not find any traces of life, either human beings or animals. I completed my question to you now, in order for you to understand why I put this question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have no problem with you putting the question. I have a problem with you characterising him as an eye-witness. Are you -- do you hear me, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hear and understand you, Your Honour. That was the way I understood what the witness was saying, that he was there on the spot and saw certain matters for himself. That's why I called him an eye-witness in terms of what he was able to see there after the operation in the wake of the operation. He was not an eye-witness to the operation itself, at Medak pocket, but he was able to see for himself what the situation was in the immediate aftermath of the operation. That was what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. McElligott, were you an eye-witness to the incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went there subsequent to it and saw the site as it was then. It was totally destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Milovancevic, you have now been cleared. Characterise the witness correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. McElligott, based on what you experienced and saw there on the spot, after the operation, would you agree with the characterisation by General Jean Cot who served with UNPROFOR and who in mid-September toured the area and said that the devastation was systematic, deliberate and full, that there were no traces of life whatsoever living, human beings or animals. Would you agree with him?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was absolute destruction. And I understand actually that one lady or female was found in a car following the first contacts of a search. She was there wounded. But there was absolute destruction, yeah, unbelievable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before you proceed, Mr. Milovancevic, I want to correct something that looks correct on the face of it but is incorrect. Line 12, page 10, I didn't say you characterised the witness correctly. I said, "Do characterise him correctly." I just want that line to be corrected. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: With regard to these two examples that you have just mentioned for us, is my next question -- my next question is relative to your last sentence in paragraph 6. We expected that the parties would negotiate and that -- and that they would reach an agreement on coexistence within Croatia and that those who had been displaced would return to their homes. The agreement on coexistence, did you consider this to be one of the goals of your mission, the mission of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was part of the Vance, Plan but it would be fair to say at the time I was there, it was something you would see on the horizon. It was an issue that perhaps one would see achieved through diplomacy, and I don't think any of the parties had got to the stage of being at that level, I think. The mission just had not got there. It was on the ground, still one of conflict and I suppose trying to keep a barrier for want of a loose word, between the parties. I suppose we were there as a buffer basically to slow things down and, it was basically at that stage, it was certainly the diplomacy end of it was a long way from a solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your own personal experience that you gathered on the ground, do you believe that the agreement on coexistence within Croatia would have been possible for the Serbs, given the description of the Croatian authorities. Would that have been a logical choice? If you think that my question is of a speculative nature and that your answer would call for speculation, you don't need to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is indeed speculative. Now I'm not quite sure where the description of the Croat authorities is given for the witness to find.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, in your view, the operation Maslenica in January 1993 and the operation Medak pocket, where the attacks of the Croatian army under the control of the Croatian authorities, if I put it this way to you, would you think that this is beyond any doubt or there is any doubt about that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I would go back to first principles and say that if we take the Vance Plan as the foundation stone for going forward at that time, and that it was adhered to in the detail, and I referred earlier to the policing component being armed in a manner not in keeping with the plan, that perhaps if we turn the clock back and started with that in mind, I think more could be achieved. The policing element of it was, I would feel, vital to securing the confidence of the minority communities, be it the Croatian or Serb, and I think it would have made a difference if we started on the correct footing. I'm not sure -- like, I know that there is a deep-rooted hurt on all sides, but I feel that, you know, if we could bring that to a halt at that time and build the bridges along there and in a very slow way that things could be achieved. Because I know from my own experience meeting people on the ground, particularly in communities, that there were still bonds despite the ethnic differences and barriers that were created. I am aware of both Serb and Croatian people inquiring and sending greetings to those on the other side of the divide and asking monitors to do it for them, if they met with them. So there was a possibility of making progress. I have no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned the armed Serbs the second time as a possible problem to the negotiated agreement, can we see document 333 from the 65 ter list? I believe that its number is 731. Exhibit 731. If this is document 333, can we please scroll up to the very beginning of the document? On the screen, Mr. McElligott, you can see a report and its title is "Status report on the Serbo-Croatian conflict and UNPROFOR mission." The date is 7 September 1992. It is relative to Sector South, and judging by the text, the date, you have already spoken about this document in your direct examination. Can we please look at page 3 that bears the following number in the top right corner, 6072? In the first paragraph, on that page, under 1, "Croatian military option," it says as follows: "Risks of military action to restore Croatian authority are indeed realistic. Croatian side's patience and goodwill is reaching the point of no return. They seem to react out of pure nationalism." In regard to this paragraph, I would like to ask you who is it that the Croatian authorities are reacting to out of pure nationalism?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said earlier, the Vance Plan dealt with what went on within the United Nations Protected Areas, and I think it is the happenings within there that generated further happenings outside of the area and at that stage you're looking, I suppose, as the bigger political military machines responding, and it's a hen-and-egg situation as to who moves first. So, you know, this is why I said that, you know, if we could establish the principles of the Vance Plan within the mission that confidence could be generated, and I know that military observers had liaisoned between both sides on the front lines that, indeed, they participated in keeping a certain calm and I suppose creating a certain dialogue between the differing parties on the front line. So, you know, I think that the reactions you see there are perhaps responses to what was seen as happening within the United Nations Protected Areas, so it's a hen-and-egg situation as to who starts what on a given day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I ask: The three areas, Serb villages that were referred to the Medak pocket, is it inside the area that is referred to in this paragraph or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is within the -- yes. It is within the -- within the UNPA or within the pink zone. It's within the area under the UN control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Given your answer, it is difficult to say what came first, the hen or the egg and who started the conflict. Paragraph 3 on the same page says: "Provocations and replies to the provocations are intensifying." I remind you this report dates from September 1992. And it says further on: "Pressure on the front line from Croatian increases daily under form of incursions, infiltrations of both armed groups and civilians. Clashes and incidents between militia and Croatian police are expanding daily. The confrontation might result from this -- with probable intervention of the Croatian army which would be followed by the opening of -- up of heavy arm stores to back it and mobilisation is probably ongoing overnight." With this regard, I would like to ask you as follows: This report speaks about the daily increase of pressure along the front line and the pressure is put by the Croatian side. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were always pressures, always. And they were coming from one side or the other. So it was an area of -- it was volatile at all times, and I suppose there was always a bubble sitting there to be burst. So that was the environment and I know that, you know, these, I suppose, reactions are -- are just driven by events on the day, and this again is where the civil affairs end of UNPROFOR take a role in getting involved at perhaps political level and getting drawbacks, and I have no doubt that they would have been deeply involved in those tensions and trying to get solutions at that level. So this was the environment we were in. It was one of constant tension and perhaps extreme tension at times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In order for us to understand the situation in which extreme tensions could be felt, could we please see a map which is Exhibit 724? Can this be shown on the screen? This is a map of the former Yugoslavia with its republics and with the UNPA areas. While this is being shown, Exhibit 724, that is, I will remind you, Mr. McElligott, that you explained to us that there were four UNPA areas. You also explained the borders between those UNPA areas and what those were. Now you can see the map on the screen. With regard to this map my question to you is as follows: In the left, lower corner, you can see a square in which it says what the markings of -- on the map mean, and the fourth one from the top is a curved upwards facing a line which says the line of cease-fire or something to that effect. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could the map be increased, please? We can't read this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you said that you see this, this is the fourth marking from the bottom, so this is a curved black line, the line of cease-fire, could we now see the map and can you please show us on the map where this line of cease-fire was? Let me help you. It went along the entire length of Sector East. It goes on along some parts of Sector West, and turns down wards. Could you please show us on the map exactly where this cease-fire line was on the entire territory of UNPA areas? Can we start from Sector East, please, which is somewhere in the middle of the map encircled in red pen.

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Sector West in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I meant Sector East, Mr. McElligott, which is to the right from Sector West, again encircled. Can you see that the entire Sector East is bordered by this black line? Is this the cease-fire line? Is this the front line?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just relying on the map, Your Honour, so I don't know exactly what it is, but it's defined as the front line here, based on the legend on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Am I right to say the front line, if that line is -- designates the front line, it is only to the west of the eastern area, not to the eastern part of -- eastern side of it, neither to the north or south of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hm, Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could you show us the cease-fire line on the east sector part? Can you see it? Can you point to it for us?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This I understand is what you're looking for, this area here; is that correct? Just the immediate boundary to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the black line, yes, precisely so. Thank you very much. Let's look at the other UNPA areas. Can you see that black line? Again, is that the same marking, and can you point that line to us? It's a black line that leads towards the rest of Croatia. Would you be able to describe it in those words, this black line goes towards those white areas? Am I correct in saying that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're looking at the easterly side of the Sector West, is that correct, at the southern part of it? Along here? It's where the line commences on the eastern side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Something interesting, when you say "along here," and you're pointing on the screen, we don't see ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it's not -- this line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you point to the line for us? Could you please do that, just point to the line for us? What line is that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the commencement of the line again, is it, you're looking for? No?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And from there, where does it go? Can you show us?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It continues westwards, looping around by the top of Sector North coming right down and around by the end of Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't know whether we have been of any assistance to the Trial Chamber. I don't know whether the Trial Chamber has been able to follow the way you pointed to the line, but can you please describe for us what you have just shown us? Can you do it in the following way? My question to you is: The black line that you see on the map that encircles the red areas, does it represent the cease-fire line between the Serbian side and the Croatian side? Would you say that the black line represents precisely that, the cease-fire line between the Serbs and the Croats?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the cease-fire line between the United Nations protected area and along the Croatian -- eastern side of Croatia. This would be along the edges of Sectors North and South. Is that what you're asking? It's showing up now, Your Honour, yes. There is a line. This line is the line you're referring to here? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the line that I had in mind. This is precisely what I wanted you to describe for us. My next question is as follows: Based on what you have described as the cease-fire line, is it obvious or not that the area that was called the so-called Republic of Serbian Krajina, depending on what people called it, in other words, the UNPA area, was it encircled from all sides by the territory under the control of the Croatian authorities, save for this part bordering on Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Sector North front line would be fully surrounded by Croatian territory, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does the same apply to Sector South, Mr. McElligott?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We no longer need the map on the screen. Let's go back to the document from the 65 ter list, number 333. In this document, dating from September, that was presented to you just a while ago, when you say that the pressure on the front line mounted by the Croatian side is growing daily and that it translated into incursions, infiltrations of both armed groups and civilians which leads to clashes with Milicija, when you're talking about the front line, this is the line that you're referring to, the one that you just pointed to us on the map. Am I right in saying that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the front line, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have the third page of document 333 from the 65 ter list? That's the document that we saw just a minute ago. Can we see its page number 3, number 3 page of that document? Please, page 3. In the upper right corner, the number is 6072. Can we scroll up a bit? A bit more, a bit more. I would like to see the third paragraph. Go down a bit. Yes, thank you. Now we come to the chapter entitled "Return of displaced Croats." Once you described the situation along the front line and you said that there were daily attacks by the Croatian forces against the UNPA areas. In paragraph 3 in September --

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I clarify something? I didn't talk about daily attacks. But there were attacks ongoing. I don't think I used the word "daily."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, sir. I showed you paragraph 3 on this page which says that the pressures on the front line from Croatians increased daily. Under the form of incursions, infiltrations of both armed groups and civilians. This is what I showed you and this is what I meant, but we did that, and we are moving on to the next chapter of this report under the title "Return of displaced Croats."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you read that to the witness, I tried very hard to look at the paragraph you were reading from. Can you tell us what paragraph that was? The one that talks about daily incursions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just a moment. Let's go back to the top of the page, please, on the monitor. This is third paragraph from the top of that page. Can we scroll up to the very top of the page, page 3? The third paragraph from the top, which starts with the following words -- again the same page but please show the top of the page. Go up, show the top of the page. This is it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you please read out for us the third paragraph starting with "provocations, retaliation"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Provocation, retaliation process is intensifying. Pressure on the front line from Croatians increases daily under form of incursions, infiltrations of both armed groups and civilians. Clashes and incidents between militia and Croatian police are expanding daily. The confrontation might result from this militia's like trend, with probable intervention of CA following -- followed by the opening up of heavy armed stores to back it. Mobilisation is probably ongoing overnight."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When we mentioned the front line, I showed you the map to see the front line and we saw that that front line encircled the entire Sector South. Now we can scroll down to the bottom third of page 3. This is chapter 3, "Return of displaced Croats." And at the very beginning of this document, it says that of utmost importance for the UNPROFOR is to show goodwill towards the Croatian side by a gesture and to follow the instructions of the staff, I believe that you meant the UNPROFOR staff, in order to find a model for return. However, the end of the same paragraph, it says: "If we were to go for a limited scope of return, the Croats would spread it everywhere and an uncontrolled large-scale return might lead to an escalation of war." My question to you is as follows: Were the Croatian authorities putting pressure on UNPROFOR and UNCIVPOL asking for a large-scale return of displaced persons?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before you answer, Ms. Valabhji?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: My apologise for rising, Your Honour, just to point out in this rather lengthy question, it is said that quote we saw that the front line encircled the entire Sector South. I think in the previous discussion of the front line, there was a mention of the Bosnia part, not being the -- that is the side of the RSK facing Bosnia, not being so encircled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what my learned friend is saying is absolutely correct. I did say that there was no front line on the Bosnian side. I'm talking only about the front line separating the Croat and the Serbs, and this is what I emphasised. I wanted to show where the line was when it came to Sector South. It was not my attempt to spread the front line to go towards the Bosnian side. It would have been pointless to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Keep excluding the Bosnian side as you put the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This was, however, inadvertently done. When we spoke of the front line in Sector South, Witness, is it beyond doubt, and is it quite clear, that we were referring only to the side facing Croatia, not the side facing Bosnia? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My former question to you was whether there was any pressure by the Croatian forces to make sure that the displaced persons returned, regardless of whether the conditions were there in place, and was UNPROFOR along with UNCIVPOL of the position that this course of action might lead to an escalation of the conflict and possibly its development into a war?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think what you're looking at is, there were tensions on all sides and pressures and it's obvious that that is there at that given time and I suppose what you have in the suggestion of an offer of some leeway is I suppose the diplomacy testing the ground to see is there a negotiating position to get the parties to stand off once more? And I think, you know, it's an exploratory type of approach and it is -- the reality was there was continuous pressure from all sides and it's within that environment you will have to assess the movements that are being probed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could we have page 4 of the document shown on the screen, please? On page 4, there is one line which reads as follows: That it seems that the conduct of the Croatian forces aims at bringing UNPROFOR into such a situation where it would seem to take all the responsibility, all the burden of guilt, for failures and delays. And it goes on to say that the impression is that some Croatian authorities might wish to deresponsiblise themselves by putting all the burden of guilt on UNPROFOR. Eventually, they are preparing the ground in front of the public opinion to justify possible military action as necessary due to UNPROFOR's unfulfilments, and you go on to say that the implications of pilot movements of return, and you're referring to villages, could be put against us. It says, UNPROFOR is failing in implementing the Vance Plan. The next step could easily be UNPROFOR, go home. In connection with this description of conduct exhibited by the Croatian side, is it quite clear to you that Croatia has been playing a political game in asking for Croatian displaced persons to return, that they were abusing the possibility of return in order to unjustifiably lay the blame on UNPROFOR and prepare the ground for a military action? Is this something that is quite evident from this text?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just like to clarify something. It was said that there that I say implying that I wrote this document. I did not do so. So it is a document that I'm aware of. I just wanted to clarify that, that what is quoted there is not me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I can pass comment on it on the basis of my own judgement. And I think it's fair to say that, you know, in the brokering process that -- and in the environment we were in, I think every bargaining tool and every pressure that could be applied was applied, so you know, it's part of the cut and thrust of what was going on at that time. So, you know, it's just part of that brokering that went on. But this is where diplomacy perhaps took hold again and the line was held or people drew back and you got another period of perhaps some degree of peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. McElligott, I didn't understand your answer at all. My question to you was to tell us whether the conduct exhibited by the Croatian side, which was described in detail in this UNCIVPOL report, was proof of or an illustration of the conduct of the Croatian side which abused the possibility of return of the Croatian displaced persons in order to lay the blame on UNPROFOR and set the stage for a military action. If you don't know the answer to my question, then say so. If you do know it, then please tell us what you know.

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the report is putting forward those inferences, and I think that is what they are. I don't think it's being stated as a reality but I think it's put forward as inferring that those pressures are going to be put on to us, that we are going to be made to feel guilty and I think it's, you know, it's that type of assessment that is being made.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McElligott. My next question has to do with the title to be found below this paragraph. "Margins of manoeuvre for UNPROFOR's action." Before I refer you to a portion of the text, I will remind you of the fact that on page 3, we spoke of the pressure from the Croatian side on the confrontation line, which was increasing daily, in the form of incursions, infiltrations of both armed groups and civilians. Then on the top of this page, we were talking about the pressure put on UNPROFOR to solve the problem of the displaced persons, and what comes next is the margin of manoeuvre for UNPROFOR's action. The first paragraph reads: "The situation might need to be assessed presently as a Serb war process in the former Yugoslavia and not as implementation of the Vance Plan in UNPAs." In order to make it quite clear what the first sentence reads here, I will refer you to the last paragraph on the page, and I quote: "Pressure should be concentrated on local authorities in Knin at UN's highest level showing our unwillingness to be cheated further. We might stop threatening them in a way that allows illusions of statehood and calling them ministers. We should openly state that pink zones are part of Croatia and that the bottom line of our operation is obviously using the appropriate formulation. And these are the two formulations as part of instructions." One of them is are we in the driving seat any more? And the second one is: Someone is cheating someone somewhere. My question in connection with this is: Do you believe that the margin of manoeuvre for UNPROFOR's action would be created by in fact laying the blame on the Serbs, in terms of them putting daily pressure on the confrontation line and in view of the pressure from the Croatian side on UNPROFOR with regard to the return of the displaced persons? What sort of formulations are these that come out of UNPROFOR? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before you answer, Ms. Valabhji?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, Your Honours, but I think the translation of a word that was being read, when the document was being read, the translation we got in the transcript is "threatening," whereas the document itself says, "Treating." And it's -- the sentence in the document, the second sentence, "We might stop treating them" as opposed to "threatening them."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We see that. With that correction, you may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This is exactly what the text reads here, as my learned friend stated, to stop treating them, not threatening them. With that correction, can you please answer my question, Witness?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I think we are going back and looking at, I suppose, an approach to the Serbian side at this stage and particularly Knin will be referring to what is actually taking place in the UN protected areas. And I think they are going back and saying, you know, everything is not right here either. And indeed I think the top paragraph, if I read it correctly, implies that interests may be in the greater issues outside the mission. So I think it's UNPROFOR just making a statement perhaps as well in relation to its position. So again, it's, I suppose, the diplomatic end of it, posturing perhaps, I suppose, on the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you believe that it is a proper way of proceeding, as you say, diplomatically, that you would shift the blame from the Croatian side on the Serb side, and the interpretation of the paragraph, as you gave it now, the -- or, rather, the interpretation of the conduct shown in the paragraph? Could we please see page 6071 of the document in connection with this? This is the number at the top right-hand side, 6071. Let us look at the bottom part of the page. That is fine. Thank you. Stop there. There is a title here, "Power struggle in RSK." I just started putting a question to you. The instruction as to how the Serbian side should be treated, that they should not be allowed illusions of statehood and that they should not be addressed as ministers, did this particular instruction lead to the text, "power struggle in the RSK"? It says: "Martic is the chief of a gang and not a political leader." And the last paragraph on page -- on this page: "Martic never gave us indications that he probably adhered to Vance Plan. On the contrary, he repeatedly stated in public that there would be no restoration of Croatian authority and that the cease-fire line is the border of the RSK."

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot speak for the writer in this situation, Your Honour. He is indicating there that he's in possession of certain facts in relation to what was said. I'm not in a position to say yes or no in that situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Milovancevic, would that be a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will reconvene at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Before we had the break, we spoke of the way Mr. Martic was treated in this UNCIVPOL report, as the chief of a gang, and as a person refusing to accept the Vance Plan. We will go back to the very beginning of this report now; that's to say, page 1 of document 333. And we will look at the title of the document. The title is "Report on the Serbo-Croatian conflict and UNPROFOR mission." What sort of Serbo-Croatian conflict was this? It isn't clear on the basis of this report whether this is the clash between the Croatian state and Croatian forces with Serbs who were citizens of Croatia living in an area under UN protection.

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I regard it as a report based on the United Nations protected area that the focus of the report is based on, that mission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And it's based on the conflict that is taking place between Serbs and Croats.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Within the -- and the focal point of that is the United Nations protected area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This has to do with the document we've been looking at so far, which is the UNCIVPOL report dated 7 September 1992. And with this statement of yours at the end of paragraph 6, where it was expected that the parties would start negotiating and achieving an agreement on coexistence of Serbs and Croats enabling people to return to their homes. Was it within the UNCIVPOL mandate to deal with negotiations, and how is it possible that UNCIVPOL, in its report dated 7 September 1992, should provide political instructions on how to treat one side or both sides?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, just before the witness answers, the witness explained that this is not his statement. This is a report written by somebody else and he's just interpreting it like you and I are trying to do. So to refer to it as this statement of yours at paragraph 6 is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will rephrase my question. You're right. The witness did state that this was not his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, this is basically what I'm interested in. The position presented in paragraph 6, which says that it was expected that the sides would reach an agreement on coexistence in Croatia. My question is the following: Was it your business to return Krajina within the territory of the Republic of Croatia and to take care of the coexistence involved or not? Was this the mandate of UNCIVPOL or not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that the Vance Plan was the foundation for this process, and that all parties agreed and signed off to working with it, and that is the basis of the whole issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you wish to say that the agreement on coexistence within the framework of Croatia was something that was envisaged under the Vance Plan? Is my understanding of what you said correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the word "envisaged" is the word used in the Vance Plan, and I think that looking at that word "envisaged" in relation to the environment existing at that time, as I mentioned earlier, I think we were a step removed from a diplomatic solution to a long -- and getting a long-term answer to the whole problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did not the Vance Plan envisage peacekeeping in order to create conditions for a peaceful solution to the crisis in the former Yugoslavia without any prejudice for the final outcome of the crisis? Isn't that what the Vance Plan provided for?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- if I'm correct, I understand it to provide for the peaceful return of people within Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You see, Mr. McElligott, you're not right. This isn't what the Vance Plan envisaged. In connection with this position of yours, I'd like to know the following: The fact that some countries recognised Croatia in 1992, did that fact possibly led you to think that way?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- my role was one of a police officer, serving on the mission in relation to the objectives set out to us. I'm not a politician, nor a diplomat. And I would not put myself forward as an authority in the detail of the politics. But I have referred to it coming within Croatia, and I understand that that -- that the wording of it to be that. That's my understanding of it. I haven't seen the document for a long, long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, maybe it might be helpful, now that you say that Mr. McElligott is not right, to tell him what the correct position was. And also for the Chamber to understand what the correct position from your point of view is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I will do that. It is true that the primary duty of this witness and UNCIVPOL was to maintain law and order in the area under their mission and not to find political solutions or to return the Krajina within the jurisdiction of the Croatian authorities, as the witness himself put in his statement. I tried to find out through my examination whether he, as a member of UNCIVPOL, of the United Nations forces, he acted with certain objectives and goals that went beyond his mission, in connection with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Milovancevic, you're not telling the witness what the right position was. You're now misstating again his evidence. He said earlier that it was not the responsibility of the -- of UNPROFOR or the UN civil police to maintain law and order. That was a responsibility of the local police. You are continuing to put things incorrectly to him and you're not correcting him where you say he's wrong. Just tell him where you said he was wrong in stating the Vance Plan as providing for peaceful return of people within Croatia, you said that was a wrong proposition. What was the right proposition? Or what was the right provision, rather?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. This is precisely what I will do now. Could we have, please, 65 ter document number 104 on our monitors? This is a report to the Security Council, number S23280, dated 20 December 1991, which has -- this report has three annexes. In connection with this document, could we see Annex 3 on our monitor. That's page 15 of the entire document. Therefore, 65 ter document 104. Your Honour, I apologise. Inadvertently I referred the Registrar to the wrong number. This is Exhibit 104 and not 65 ter document 104. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Registrar, are you able to give us Exhibit 104?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us look at page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. McElligott, this is the report to the Security Council dated 11 December 1991. The report is of the -- of Secretary-General in keeping with Resolution 721 from 1991. Could we please take a look at page 15 of the document? The title is "Annex 3." MSF 210-01. 003132725. That is the ERN number. While this is being shown, I'm going to read the provision from paragraph 1 of Annex 3, Mr. McElligott. Annex 3 contains the concept for the peacekeeping operation of United Nations in Yugoslavia. When it comes to the general principles, it says, under 1, the peacekeeping operation of United Nations in Yugoslavia will be an arrangement in order to create conditions for peace and security which are necessary for negotiations about the overall solution of the Yugoslav crisis. It is not going to prejudice the outcome of such negotiations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, the Chamber has been advised by registry that this document, the one that they have on e-court has got only 9 pages and there are no annexes to it. I'm not quite sure what you were reading from now when you read, because what you have called on to the screen is the report of the Secretary-General pursuant to Security Council Resolution 721 of 1991. You have not called a copy of the Vance Plan on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I see we are facing a problem. It is possible that this is our mistake. However, this is a complete document that I have in hard copy. This is the resolution of the Security Council. This document has been provided to us by the Prosecution. The resolution is number -- I apologise, this is a report of the Secretary-General of the Security Council. The number is 23280. The date is 11 December 1991. It deals with this issue. It has four annexes, and the third annex speaks about the concept of the peacekeeping operation. If it doesn't exist in e-court, then I'll have to come back later to this document. I suggest that I should proceed with my cross-examination in order to avoid wasting time. We are going to try and resolve the problem in some other way, if you're agreeable. I did not know until this very moment that there was this problem, because the whole report is a single document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In terms of the best-evidence rule, will you make please sure that you get the Vance Plan and not the Secretary-General's reports or other documents so that let us see the original document itself on what it provides, particularly on the question where you challenged the witness, the witness's understanding of the Vance Plan. Yes, suspend your further cross-examination on this issue until you have got proper documentation. You may proceed on further cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will follow that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 8 and paragraph 9, as well as in paragraph 10, Mr. McElligott, of your statement to the Prosecution, that is, you're talking about the mandate of the UNCIVPOL and you're saying that the primary duty is to maintain law and order in the mission area, and this rested with the existing police force. And you're also saying that the UNCIVPOL police force did not have any executive powers for maintaining public order. And you are also explaining that the mandate of the UNCIVPOL implied monitoring the local police under A; and under B to provide appropriate assistance to the appropriate bodies of the international organisations in a view of the return of displaced persons. With regard to this mandate of the UNCIVPOL, my first question to you is as follows: Is it clear that the mandate of the UNCIVPOL does not encompass anything to the effect of seeking a political resolution to the crisis?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand your answer well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Please go ahead. I think you're about to do the same thing as I was about to, interject in respect of Mr. Milovancevic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you say no, Your Honour, does that mean that seeking a political solution did not make part of the political mandate, or did it mean something else?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I answered in the sense of did CIVPOL have a role to play in a political solution. And we would not have regarded ourselves as the politicians in the situation. We were there to provide a specific policing role.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And one brief question: With that record, in other words, seeking a political solution for the crisis in the area under the UN mandate was not your task, was it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose I could be regarded as part of an overall team, and looking at it in a global way, I suppose, every unit played its own part in bringing what would ultimately be a political solution. So in -- I suppose everybody contributed in some way, be it minor or otherwise, in generating what would be finally a political solution. But the police force would not have a leading role, perhaps. Let's put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that the police did play a role in seeking a political solution, although it may not have been a leading role, as you say? And what role was that, if any?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll go back to our organisational structure and look at how we functioned, and we reported to the director of civil affairs, who had a direct responsibility -- or responsibility for directing the political and civil affairs end of the mission. So we would have reported into them. So that would be the line of command within the organisation. So, you know, we were -- civil affairs had the political end of the business to deal with. And that is where we backed away and they took up their position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can Exhibit 115 be shown, please. The document that is being shown is Vance's plan, Mr. McElligott. Can we go to page 5, 01145413 is the indication on that page. Can we please zoom in on the left page and can we scroll down to the chapter entitled "Basic concept," and can you please read the text under bullet 7, Mr. McElligott? Can you do that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The United Nations troops and police monitors would be deployed in certain areas of Croatia designated as United Nations Protected Areas. These areas would be demilitarised, all armed forces in them would be either withdrawn or disbanded. The role of the United Nations troops would be to ensure that the area remained demilitarised and that all persons residing in them were protected from fear of armed attack. The role of the United Nations police monitors would be to ensure that the local police forces carried out their duties without discrimination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. McElligott, can you please read slowly when you're reading? And can you finish the reading by reading the rest of the text on the following page? You finished with "without discrimination." Against whom?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Persons of any nationality abusing anyone's human rights. As the United Nations force assumed its responsibilities in the United Nations Protected Areas, UNPAs, all JNA forces deployed elsewhere in Croatia would be relocated outside the republic. The United Nations force would also, as appropriate, assist the humanitarian agencies of the United Nations in the return of all displaced persons who so desired to -- who so desired to their homes in the UNPAs."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we scroll down and display the entire paragraph 8 and can the witness please read the last sentence in that paragraph? The last sentence preceding bullet number 9. Starting with "as already" --

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're looking at: "The UNPAs would be areas in Croatia in which the Secretary-General judged" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but just the last sentence in that bullet.

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: "As already stated, the special arrangements in these areas would be an interim -- of an interim nature and would not prejudge the outcome of political negotiations for the comprehensive settlement in the Yugoslav crisis."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McElligott. I apologise for having asked you to read this. It is not easy to read from the monitor. However, does it transpire from the text that you have just read out --

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Just to point out that earlier my learned colleague, at page 30 of the transcript, line 17, told the witness that he was not correct when he started to answer regarding the question on the Vance Plan, and I think for the record that this document indicates that he is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Valabhji. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the document speaks about the role of the civilian police of the United Nations, and if it says verbatim that this arrangement in the Owen's plan would not prejudge the outcome of political negotiations for a comprehensive settlement of the Yugoslav crisis, do you consider that your statement that Vance's plan envisaged the reintegration of the Serbian areas in Croatia is something that is contrary to these provisions of Vance's plan?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I don't understand which way you're going, but before I say what I want to say, your learned friend was on her feet. Let's hear what she's got to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just wonder could my learned friend point me to the part of the statement that he's referring to? I am not getting it, frankly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the document that we have on the screen now is the document that has been shown to the witness to help him provide an answer with the statement that we see in the last sentence of paragraph 6 of his statement to the Prosecutor's office. And which is connected with his further explanation. And that is that it was expected that the two sides would negotiate and that they would reach an agreement of coexistence within Croatia. And he also referred to the provisions of Vance's plans envisaging something like that. Now I have shown the document that speak about the negotiations and the special arrangements would not prejudge the outcome of political negotiations. And my question is: Whether his position is prejudging the outcome of political negotiations and is that the way how he perceived the role of his mission or his mission as such.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I followed the mandate as it was given to us by the United Nations at the time. I'm now looking -- raising an event 13 years later and, well, detail at this point, I can see where a misunderstanding can arise. And on looking at paragraph 8, it does say that the UNPAs would be areas in Croatia in which the Secretary-General judged that special arrangements were required. So I'm conscious of that. And the final wording there does leave the door open for a negotiated solution. But it didn't certainly influence my thoughts one way or the other on how I should do my job in the mission. I was conscious of the detail of the plan then and worked to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It may just be that maybe I've been a little amiss, or remiss, rather. I don't have a copy of your statement to the Prosecutor, and this reference to this paragraph 6 is what I'm interested in because I want to see how it differs with what is in the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the representative of the Registry to provide the Trial Chamber with a copy of that document, i.e., item 6 of that statement. I know that it was shown to the witness before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. While we are waiting for that, what I do want to raise with you, Mr. Milovancevic, is that the witness has been saying to you all the time that it was not for his section to negotiate a settlement but he reported to higher command in the -- in the chain of command within UNPROFOR, and all he saw was what they were doing, each one in a way was contributing towards a settlement, a negotiated settlement, and, of course, the contribution by the UN police is quite clear. They were creating conditions in which such negotiation could take place, by separating the parties. Now, I'm not quite sure what it is you are fighting with about -- you are fighting with him about. But maybe once I've got the paragraph 6 of his statement, I may see the contradiction.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have some hard copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would appreciate a copy. Thank you so much. I've read his paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you for your question. We have dwelt upon this quite for sometime. What we are trying to verify is how the witness, as a high official of UNCIVPOL perceived the role of UNCIVPOL. We want to make inferences from that as to how he worked on the ground and what his attitude towards the problem was. This is what I'm trying to get from the witness, actually. We have received answers from the witness, and if you will allow me to do, I may proceed with my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you proceed, I'm sorry, I want to follow where you're going. The witness states clearly how he understands the mission of the UN Civil Police in paragraph 6 of his statement to the OTP. He has been telling us from the last two days how he acted on the ground. I would like you to point us to a contradiction, if that's your contention, between his behaviour on the ground and his understanding of the mission, or whatever contradiction it is that -- or inconsistency that it is that you want to point us to. If you are saying that he's misconstrued the Vance Plan, show us how. If you are saying he did not act in terms of the Vance Plan, show us how so that we follow you. As it is now, the last couple of questions you have been putting to him, I'm not able to follow you. And my inability to follow you is now reinforced after reading paragraph 6 of his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. McElligott, the expectations that you speak about in paragraph 6 that an agreement would be reached on coexistence within Croatia, does it arise from the provisions of the Vance Plan that you have just read out for us?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Vance Plan --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you answer --

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object. I think that my learned colleague is now misquoting the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: He says -- he refers to expectations in paragraph 6 of the statement that an agreement would be reached on coexistence within Croatia. The line in the statement says: "It was envisaged that the parties would negotiate and reach an agreement of coexistence within Croatia and that those who had been displaced would return to their homes." We've already looked at the text of the Vance Plan in the document that was just pulled up, 01145413, in which the return of displaced persons is specifically referred to, so there is no contradiction in this regard; and second, he merely refers to what was envisaged. There is no question of prejudging the outcome or forcing an outcome or anything of this kind. It's merely what was envisaged at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just to add on to what counsel has just mentioned, Mr. Milovancevic, that very sentence that talks of being -- something being envisaged, I would like you to take note of the fact that what was envisaged was that the parties themselves, not UNPROFOR, the parties themselves, would negotiate and reach an agreement. So UNPROFOR was not party to that negotiation. That's what I would like to emphasise to you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question about this topic, Mr. McElligott. Your expectations about the outcome of political negotiations were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where do these expectations come from? Where does he talk about his expectations? We have just read that the plan envisaged that the parties would negotiate an agreement, but he's not part of the plan. He's just implementing that portion of the plan that was within his area of jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'll proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you're talking about the mandate of the United Nations police, you're saying that it is to -- that the primary responsibility maintaining law and order in the mission area rested with the existing police forces, and the UNCIVPOL police force did not have executive powers but to monitor the local police, to ensure that they carry out their task without discrimination and to provide the appropriate assistance to the United Nations in assisting with the return of refugees. When it comes to the monitoring of the local police, you're talking about the monitoring role of the UNCIVPOL. This role of the UNCIVPOL, did it actually represent a typically policing work on the ground? I mean the way it is described under these two bullet points.

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: One has to put it in the context of the environment of the day, and again, the foundation stone for it is the Vance Plan, which was drawn up taking full cognizance of that environment. So, you know, we were dealing with a difficult situation, and we monitored it on the basis that the respect that were due to people's rights should be given to them. And I don't think you can walk away from that, no matter what the circumstances are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But as I understood you, your testimony yesterday, or I beg your pardon, last Friday, you talked of either people reporting incidents to you or you yourself observing incidents and then writing or communicating with those of the police on either side who you thought could control the situation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And in that respect you wrote several letters to Mr. Martic and other authorities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Letters were written to the various departments --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So that was the manner in which you were monitoring.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the -- we monitored, we established facts and then reported on, and if an issue arose to make complaint.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You reported and asked for action to be taken.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and it was done at different levels. Perhaps at some occasions it was done at station level, district level. And, you know, at a more serious level, it went to effectively government. Let's put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think that explains the monitoring that he says -- and I think this came from his testimony on Friday, Mr. Milovancevic. Maybe you may want to cross-examine him along that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was precisely coming to that topic, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When in paragraph 10, under items A to N, you list the monitoring duties vis-a-vis the local police forces, those duties, were those duties belonging to the UNCIVPOL police monitors? Was -- were these the duties that they themselves had to discharged?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In order to describe the way UNCIVPOL carried out its duties on the ground, you presented the UNCIVPOL structure, that's page 5 in the B/C/S version, starting with paragraph 13, and according to this UNCIVPOL structure, there is one formal chain of command, as you called it. I have one question in connection with this formal chain of command. Is it true that police monitors operated on the ground as the basic structure of UNCIVPOL, that they were answerable to the station commander of UNCIVPOL, that the UNCIVPOL station commander was answerable to the chief of the sector, that the sector chief was answerable to the UNCIVPOL commissioner in Zagreb, and that the UNCIVPOL commissioner was answerable through the chief of mission in Zagreb to the structure above? Was that the actual chain of command?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the line of command or was the line of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that in line with the organigramme that you showed us on Friday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 12, you explain that upon your arrival at UNCIVPOL headquarters, you were appointed chief -- head of operations and then Chief of Staff and deputy commissioner in charge of operations. There you go on to describe the duties you had. Can you tell us: In what particular periods of time you were head of operations, then Chief of Staff, and deputy commissioner?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure of the dates. When I arrived at the mission, I filled the vacancy of head of operations, and subsequent to that, the person who was Chief of Staff rotated home. Perhaps that could have been somewhere into -- it would have been somewhere into the new year, 1993, and a further rotation took place then when the deputy commissioner, the Jordanian, went home and I filled that vacancy or was appointed to that vacancy. So, you know, it all happened within a 12-month period.
