But time-wise, probably you could have maybe three or four months of a period in operations, maybe the same, and then a further period as the deputy, so they all extended somewhere about four months, there, thereabouts somewhere, range in that area. But they are all based on rotation, taking place within the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were your duties in all three posts to analyse incidents in the area UNCIVPOL was responsible for?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as head of operations and the deputy commissioner I certainly would be looking at incidents. Chief of Staff was more focussed on our resources or the human and the logistical side of the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: According to the UNCIVPOL organigramme we were looking at on Friday, which is Exhibit 722, it follows that the analysis of the incident was only within the duties of deputy commissioner and commissioner himself.

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The role of head of operations came within the line of command to the deputy commissioner; in other words, that office was the operational side of the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could we look at Exhibit 722 on our monitors, which is the UNCIVPOL structure? This diagram shows that deputy commissioner analyses incidents, so deputy commissioner is in charge of incident analysis. Does it follow from this organisational diagram that you were able to carry out incident analysis while holding all the three posts that you had?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: As Chief of Staff, I was not directly involved in operations, but each morning we -- a meeting was held with the commissioner and his key staff, so I was privy to, I suppose, everything that was happening on the field at all times. But when I was Chief of Staff the focus was on the human resource and the logistical side of the mission. But as I say, each day I was in touch.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In other words, incident analysis was not, strictly speaking, your line of business but you were informed of the findings thereof. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a staff attached to both offices with an overall staff of, I think, 18 at the headquarters, and a number of them were deployed on the operational side and a number on the Chief of Staff side, which would be administrative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I ask you a question? Does head of operations, as you mention at paragraph 12, mean the same thing as chief of operations as listed on the organigramme just below deputy commissioner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is, yes, same -- same -- talking about the same situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. McElligott, in chapter UNCIVPOL sectors, paragraph 14 to 17, you speak of the four sectors, Sector North, Sector South, Sector East, Sector West. In all the four sectors, you also mention the places where the sectors were based. You also mention UNCIVPOL stations. Can it be said that the total of 32 UNCIVPOL stations were located in the four sectors?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a further chart showing where each station is located and through the sector. So the detail is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A simple count of these stations mentioned in paragraphs 14 to 17 arrives at the total of 32 UNCIVPOL stations. Let me ask you the following: This disposition of UNCIVPOL stations, does it indicate that -- or does it mean that a given number of police monitors, about 500 of them, went out of each and every one of these stations every day, to monitor the situation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not so. The police staff we had about I think is 18 or 20 I mentioned for headquarters. Each headquarters section would have a small staff to administer the sector. Monitors would work over a 20 -- a seven-day week, so rest days had to be calculated in on the basis that they got a certain amount of rest time, and indeed shift work could also deplete that strength somewhat more on the basis that you could have one shift starting at, say, 7.00 a.m. and finishing at 3.00 or 4.00 and another starting at 3.00 p.m. and going to a later hour, or starting earlier and overlapping so that you don't have the entire staff working at all times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But did you have 500 police monitors per station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had I think about 460 in all -- overall for the entire mission. Or 640. 640, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That would be considerably less than 500 per station.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely. Stations would vary. But again we have a chart there, a chart showing the actual strength in each station throughout the mission. I think you can range from five to somewhat more, but it was a low staffing level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have Exhibit 723 on our monitors? These are UNCIVPOL stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When I put a question to you in connection with the paragraphs where you described UNCIVPOL's structure, I was referring to the UNCIVPOL stations that are to be found in this particular diagram; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please let us look at Exhibit 725 now. When we look at document 0810, that's the page, we have Sector East here and the figure of monitors, that's to say, the number of monitors there is 138. If we could take a look at the -- could we have -- could we take a look at the document below, exactly? Could you scroll up a bit? Could we look at the last line, bottom left? We have a figure there, I believe it's 138. That's the total number of monitors; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Total number of monitors for? For a station, a sector?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For a sector, Sector East, I understand it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could we look at the next page, please? That's page 0811. Could we also take a look at the last line, at the bottom, where the total number of monitors for Sector North is listed? Do you see the figure? How many monitors were there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's somewhat clouded. I think it's 167 as I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we take a look at the next page? That's page 0812. The bottom left-hand corner shows that there were 127 monitors in Sector South, as far as I'm able to make out. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The next page, 813, in the bottom left-hand corner, the figure for the total number of monitors in Sector West is 121.

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In connection with the total number of monitors -- or, rather, when we add up all these figures of monitors, we arrive at a figure of about 500. You stated there were 5 or 8 or 10 of these monitors in each of the stations, depending on the situation, and these were be actually the persons going out into the field. My question is: Did the UNCIVPOL police stations write reports every day on the basis of the information they gathered in the field?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. A report was prepared each day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 21 of your statement, you state that police monitors in various stations submitted daily reports on the incidents they recorded and all these reports were then compiled into one single report. Does it mean that all the reports arriving from all the different UNCIVPOL police stations were then compiled into a single report? For instance, all the police stations in Sector South provided their respective reports, which would then be integrated into a single report? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: A single report was provided -- was produced at CIVPOL headquarters each night, and it set out all incidents of note on the report for the commissioner. It was available each morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I have the following question: If there were 32 police stations on the ground, let us take this figure as the correct one, although we can arrive at the correct figure, does it mean that every day 32 reports were made which originated from every single police station?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each station submitted a report to its headquarters and they then prepared a consolidated report from those documents. So at headquarters we received a report from each sector headquarters. We did not receive all the individual reports. We just received a single report from a district -- from a headquarters office in a sector. So, in other words, we would receive a report from Sector North, south, east, west, Sarajevo, so forth, Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question I think that's being put to you is each one of these police stations, on a daily basis, submitted a report to its sector headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And the sector headquarters would then coordinate all those reports and send them to the main head office in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's what we were asking. Proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: All these questions had to do with paragraphs 14, 15, 16 and 17. There were four UNCIVPOL sectors, north, south, east, west. When all the reports coming from all the police stations were submitted, each of the sectors would produce a consolidated report, and then each of the sectors would send their consolidated reports to headquarters in Zagreb. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 22, you also explain that when these consolidated reports from the four sectors arrived, every night a duty officer attached to my office at Zagreb prepared an overall situation report of -- on the basis of all the reports received from the sector chiefs. Does this mean that on the basis of all these 32 reports that were initially submitted and consolidated into four reports, a final, overall UNCIVPOL report would be produced in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know which criteria guided the duty officer in selecting relevant from the overall issues and discarding irrelevant issues? Was he governed by his own discretion, or did he have rules to be governed by, or was there something else?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were guidelines in the preparation of the reports, and again the people who are there were people of experience, so that again I had access and indeed we had access to all the reports, so we had an opportunity to review what was coming to him as well from time to time, so we were in the position to make a judgement call on the correctness or otherwise of what was being done. So there was an evaluation taking place independent of guidelines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know whether the guidelines were informed by the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They would be based on the -- the foundation would be the Vance Plan, and the guidelines in reporting would come from ourselves based on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah. But they would be informed by what the Vance Plan requires of you to do on the ground.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter document 324 on our monitors? This is a situation report for Sector South of CIVPOL, 29 May 1992 is the date, sent to the sector commander, commander of the UN forces, General Nambiar, 65 ter document 324. The document you have before you, sir, do you recognise it as a document normally drafted by UNCIVPOL regardless of the headquarters in this case, it's the headquarters of Sector South?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. It's been produced already. I have read it already.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the penultimate paragraph on this page, could we please scroll it up a bit to see the end of the page, the penultimate paragraph, yes, please, stop there. Below the title "Operations," it states: "During our first two months here, the local population were optimistic." Have you found that portion?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: "During our first two months here, the local population were optimistic that UNPROFOR would help and protect the local community." This report is dated 29 May 1992. And then, on the next page, bearing the number 5826, there is the title "Expulsion of Croats" there. You -- or I apologise, not you, but the author of this report writes: "Every effort has been made by CIVPOL to ensure their safety within the UNPA Sector South," and they are referring to Croats. The second sentence reads: "Despite these efforts by CIVPOL to ensure their safety, the local Milicija are continuing to undermine and intimidate these people." At the end of this text you're referring to an annex which deals with such incidents. In connection with this portion of the text entitled "Expulsion of Croats," can you tell us whether such a conclusion reported in such a report, which is apparently a monthly report, is that the work product that would be produced by the section commander upon receiving -- by the station commander, upon receiving various reports from police stations?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you clarify the question again, please? Apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. McElligott. The question might have been a bit long. When somebody drafts a report covering a one-month period, would that be a report which deals -- which is written by an officer or a person in charge of the analysis of material, and this is the type of material that you're talking about when you talk about the submission of reports in the headquarters in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report, as I understand, was prepared by Sameer, Bino. He's a Jordanian, and I suppose -- his mother tongue is not English, and it is prepared in the light of that. But it is -- he's setting out a position there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it a monthly report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would just like to look at the top again, please. Could I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can the Registrar please show us the top of the document, the heading of the document? Maybe while the Registrar is looking for the heading of the document, we might perhaps take a break, and then answer the question when we come back. Court adjourned and come back --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic? I see your opposite number is standing.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Yes, my apologies for interjecting at this stage, Your Honour, but I just wanted to bring up the issue of the length of cross-examination. At this stage, it would start to exceed the length of the direct exam, and I would just recall the Chamber's -- Trial Chamber's guidelines, paragraph 11 which says that the principle is that the time principally should not exceed the time allotted for the examination-in-chief unless there are particular circumstances requiring an extension. We would submit that there are no particular circumstances and that we would ask that the cross be completed in time so as to allow time for redirect and for Your Honours' questions today, all today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Prosecutor has introduced a number of documents through this witness, some of them of a tens of pages long. The witness spoke about only some of those pages, and made inferences based on those pages. And now we are being told that we should limit our cross-examination. We are aware of the principle of the equal length of time. However, the witness is very important. He testifies about a period covering a year, and the Prosecutor has had a very easy job. He has shown the witness a document and asked him to confirm things. I believe that we will be able to finish our cross-examination tomorrow, sometime after the first session, and we would kindly request the Trial Chamber to allow us to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, one thing that militates against the Trial Chamber agreeing to that is the fact that your questions are inordinately long, and whatever you say before you finally put your question is invariably not related to the question as such and it's just repetitive of the evidence. I would ask you to - which is also something that is in the guidelines - to please just put your questions to the witness without giving a long speech each time you ask him a question. That way we probably can finish quicker. Proceed, Mr. Milovancevic. Just go straight to cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I shall follow your instruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. McElligott, we left it off with the report written in May 1991 of Sector South [indiscernible] to the commander of the United Nations. This is a summary report. And my last question to which I would kindly ask to you answer is this: Is this a summary report based on individual reports written about the situation on the ground?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the report written by the sector commander outlining the situation on a given date and it's addressed to the force commander, so it hasn't gone through the normal chain of command for the CIVPOL side. I think it's an assessment. And it sets out a number of points in relation to the establishment of the mission on that date, and he made, I think, two notable points in relation to one, the concerns of the local -- or the expectations, I think, of the local population, and the situation in relation to the minority population as well. So it's not a normal daily situation report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we see the next page of the document; 5827, that is. This report is relative to the expulsion of Croats, and it refers to the annex which contains such incidents. The annex is on the following page, and it contains a series of areas, Benkovac, Obrovac, the area of Knin, again Benkovac, Benkovac, and it speaks about individual cases. For example, in the first case, it says that armed bandits attacked the Croatian population in Zelici and also that on the 12th of May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... don't read what is already there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you believe that the information contained in chapters relative to Obrovac and Benkovac, looking from the bottom of the page, the second and third line from the bottom of the page, do you think that it is possible for such a report to the UNPROFOR mission to reach him and is it a realistic report? It says that 12 artillery shells were fired on Benkovac on the 24th of May, that they fell on the town, that somebody was injured, a woman was injured, and that for Obrovac on the same day the 24th of May, again 12 projectiles fell on the ground inflicting somewhat less damage. Is this part of the incident report something that could be left out from a report to the commander of the forces, in your view?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Sorry, there are two questions there. There are two questions there, which you have asked the witness. Could you address the first question and then could the witness answer the second question? Because there are very much two questions there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And while you ask the first question, let me just remind you that this witness's beliefs have nothing to do with this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, since this report did not go through the regular processing of the UNCIVPOL we will not insist. I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraphs 25 and 26 of your statement, you are talking about crimes committed against Croats, in parentheses, murders, thefts, and you said that you were shown a report dated the 27th of July, 1993 in which the specific cases are discussed. In paragraph 26, you mention a list of the specific killings that happened in various places. And in connection with this, you make an inference that in your view, those were intentional and deliberate acts, the acts of intimidation, that it's aimed at achieving a high degree of publicity in order to force entire families to move out. My question to you is as follows: Do you know, has it been established for any of these killings, who the perpetrators were? This is not clear from the report.

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are a number of incidents mentioned, and while they are not in front of me I believe that there is mention of men in uniform mentioned as suspects for them. This is my recollection, and I don't have the detail. But the view I expressed was that they were deliberate. I think -- some of them were killings, I think, in some instances. I again don't have the detail, but I think there are more than one person killed; indeed, people killed in their homes. So you know that -- and, again, very elderly people. So that I did express a strong view that they were very deliberate. In fact, I think the details would be that they were executions, you know. I would like to look at each one, if it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can the report number 327 from 65 ter list be shown, please? This is an UNCIVPOL report dated 27 July 1993. Could we go to page marked as 7039? On page 7039, before it appears on the screen, it says, under the title "Crimes committed by Croats," [as interpreted] that in the area of UNCIVPOL station in Drnis, there was a killing with -- a murder of eight victims. Can we see please page 7039 of this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to correct something. The transcript that we see here says as to the document's title crimes committed by Croats but in fact the document reads "Crimes committed against" -- I'm sorry, the transcript says "Crimes committed by Croats" but the document reads "Crimes committed against Croats in Sector South."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The title is "Crimes committed against Croats from February 1993 to present," and the first part speaks about Drnis station UNCIVPOL in February 1993. There is a list of eight victims. And then in the summary it says: "All of the above-mentioned individuals were found shot in the kitchen of Bracic Ivan's house, with the exception of Josip Parac."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, in reading that report what is your question to the witness? You are wasting the time. You are the person who says you need more time to question the witness. Put the question to the witness, please. He can read -- this is a literate witness. He can read this -- the statement. You have referred him to the page. Put the question --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you see that the crime was committed by people in uniform, and does it transpire from this document who the perpetrators of the crime was? That is my question to you, Mr. McElligott.

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this specific incident - the whole screen is not open - but I just got a glance, I don't think there were any suspects that were found. The point I'm making in that is that you're looking at, you know, a family, elderly people killed in their home, and that is a deliberate act in the sense that everybody in that place was killed. I think you cannot get more deliberate than that, and I think the impact of that in the community is absolutely devastating. It would send shock waves anywhere. And I understand I have a number of those mentioned in expressing the view that I did express.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are any uniformed people mentioned in the report in connection with this crime or not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this specific one, no, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: If you don't know who the perpetrators were, how can you speak about their motives? How can you say that their motive is to gain maximum publicity and that their motive is to force other families to flee? How can you be sure of that? This is a possible inference, but what do you base your inference on?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have looked at the overall number that I have selected, and on the basis of an examination of those I've expressed the view. I didn't base it on an individual one, but I have cited a number and based my view on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we please look at page 7057, relative to the murder of Pero Palinic in Sonkovic? The case is under January 1993, and it says here that one person, a member of the border police, was arrested by the police in connection with this case, but there was not enough proof to resolve the case. Does this situation point to the fact that the Martic's police or Republic of Srpska Krajina, or anybody else for that matter, had anything to do with the case, in your view?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, it's a single case and again there is a border militiaman mentioned as a suspect. It stops short of that. That's -- could say that the case didn't advance beyond that. And, again, I would take it as one of the group I have selected. And, again, the age profile is a very old person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can page 7071 be shown, please? This is relative to the murder of 11 persons from Medvidja. Once this page appears on the monitor, you will see, Mr. McElligott, that this is a page relative to the Benkovac station of UNCIVPOL. And if you have it before you now, which you do, you will see that the names of the victims are not known. The fact that the head of the police confirmed that there were 11 murders in that area of Benkovac and even provided the family names of these people, does this fact in your view show that the police was actively involved in elucidating those cases, that they were working on resolving those cases?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were cases --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you testifying now, Mr. Milovancevic, or is it the witness who is testifying?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm asking the witness whether such a report means that to him or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you drop down the case again, please, or the summary? Again, it's based on the title, crimes against Croats, and it's a summary, and I have no doubt when those who wrote it did it that it was a crime against Croatians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What I asked you, Mr. McElligott, was whether the fact that the head of the police in Benkovac, i.e., the head of the police station of the MUP of the RSK, confirms that there were 11 murders, that he had the family names of the victims, which you didn't have, does this fact point to the fact that the police was actively involved in elucidating those cases?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the police were aware of the case, yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we go to page 7072? Speaking about the murder of four Croats from Donja Jagodnja. This is the first case on that page. Looking from the top of the page, the date is 18 March 1993. Four persons are mentioned here. It says in the report that the CIVPOL received confidential information that four Croats had been murdered in that village and the house was set on fire. The information that exists in the report, will it provide you with any kind of insight as to who did that, whether they were civilians or uniformed personnel, where they came from? Is there any information in the report pointing to any of those?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... again, you have four -- a number of elderly people killed in their home. So it's the killing of multitudes, you know, in a single location shows that it's a clear deliberate plan to kill. One has to look at the consequences of it and the impact that it has on those surrounding it. It's in that context I make my comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The deliberate plan by unknown perpetrators, can you put a link between those cases, Mr. Martic and the police of the RSK? Based on this report and information contained herein, can you establish that link at all?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your Honour, the questions that have been put to the witness on this document refer to certain specific incidents, and now a question is being asked as to the whole report. However, we haven't gone through all of the incidents that are referred to in this report. So I think that the question misstates the evidence, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic, any response?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question to the witness was as follows, Your Honours: Do the data on the specific incident and the concrete victims provide the witness with an ability to infer that these cases had anything to do with the police of the Republic of Srpska Krajina or Mr. Martic present here? The question was very concrete, and it is relative to the general conclusion by the witness that this is the evidence for the policies that were being implemented in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Wait a minute, Mr. Milovancevic. Now you're asking -- you're making two contradictory statements. You say the data on the specific incident and the concrete victims provided the witness with an ability to infer that these cases had anything to do with the police of the Republic of Srpska Krajina, or Mr. Martic. Then that's being very specific. You're talking about the specific incidents you have dealt with. Then you go on, the question was very concrete, and it is relative to the general conclusion. It can't go to the general conclusion if you're talking about just those specific -- this is the very purpose of the objection. The objection is you seek to draw a general conclusion from this witness based on a few incidents without having gone through the whole report. Now, if you want him to comment on those specific incidents, ask him to do so. If you want him to comment on the general conclusion, then lay a basis for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In regard to this specific case of the four dead bodies in Donja Jagodnja, can you please tell me who the perpetrators were? Do you have that information?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... reports, Mr. Milovancevic, no suspects and no arrests. How can he tell you who the perpetrators are?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since this is just one of the cases, a case that was chosen by the witness and was used in his statement as an illustration of the general politics and the general climate that prevailed at the time, I'm just reading his statement. My question is relative both to the specific case and the general conclusion. I'm asking him about the specific case at the moment. Since there was an objection, I will rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, among the four victims, Zarkovic, Milan is a Serb. Is the witness aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that is stated there. Which report, 82/93, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This is at the very top of the page. And the report is 82/93.

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. No suspects, no arrests.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. We'll move on. Can 7076, please, be shown, dealing with the murder of the Ivkovic couple? This case was listed under S459/92. Have you been able to locate it, Mr. McElligott? Two persons were murdered in Dobropoljci on the 1st or 2nd of October, 1992. Can you see that, first?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's Ivan and Stevanija; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. In this case, the victims include one Serb and one Croat. They were shot to death.

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does the report clearly indicate that the police launched an investigation, and do you know who it was who reported the incident to the police? Does it transpire from this report?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't transpire from the report. But, again, if it's -- I'm basing it on those who have been killed. I think you have a Croat, a male, and the female, who is a Serb married to a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could we please take a look at page 7082? The last case on the page, at the very bottom of the page, the victims are Arbanas family. There are several victims. The first person is a female Serb married to a Croat; the rest are Croats. Does this report show whether UNCIVPOL reported the incident to the RSK police or in fact no inference can be drawn to that effect?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This summary report does not state that. This report is just a summary of all the incidents, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In this particular case --

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. If I'm not mistaken, the summary we just looked at may continue to the next page, if I'm reading this correctly; that is, the top of 7083.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Valabhji. You see that Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I was just about to refer Mr. McElligott to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Under the title "Summary" on the next page, involving this same case, and that's page 7083, it is stated that the police conducted an investigation but that no suspects were identified. Do you know whether the launching of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, the report does show that the incident was reported to the RSK police and that's why they are investigating. That was your question to the witness. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On this same page, there is the case involving the murder of family Mirinovic which took place on the 2nd of December, 1992. That's at page 7083. It is evident from this report that the police conducted an investigation. Is that quite clear, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... refer to, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us look at the next page, which is murder at Rastevic, page 7084. In this case, a husband and a wife were murdered by unknown persons. Can one conclude on the basis of the report whether there was an investigation or not? Do you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of this report, it's silent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When in paragraph 27 you state in reference to all these specific cases, but you're speaking generally about them, that these were acts of extreme and ruthless intimidation, and indeed they were. However, where not a single perpetrator was identified or the perpetrators' motives for such acts, do you have any basis to tie these cases up with the actions of the accused by merely referring to them?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are a sequence of extremely serious crimes committed in a community. And they have -- would have an absolutely horrifying impact on anyone surrounding it, and particularly when they are all directed at a particular ethnic group, they will rebound back to those people. Now, have I connections with them? I didn't make any specific connection, I think, when I made the observation in that particular point, but taking the overall situation I think I strengthened that further as I go, but I just refer to them as obvious acts of serious intimidation and that is what I would see them as.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the next paragraph, which is expulsion of Croats from the RSK -- my apologies, I didn't switch the microphone on. Your next chapter in the text is entitled "Expulsion of Croats from RSK." And then in paragraphs 28 and 29, you provide an explanation of the title. In doing so, you refer again to the report dated 27 July 1993. Could we please take a look at the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Senior counsel has reminded me that the witness probably doesn't have his statement in front of him, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank my learned friends from the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 28, Mr. McElligott, you quote the report dated 27 July, which is 65 ter document 327. You also quote 65 ter document 345, which we will deal with later on. And you state in paragraph 29: "Trends from the reports I've been shown indicate that the special police were actively intimidating and expelling Croats." Could we have document 327, that's 65 ter document 327, and the pages are -- the page is 7063. As proof of the fact that the special police, as you put it -- therefore, as trends from the reports indicating that the special police were actively intimidating and expelling Croats, you also refer to this particular page, 7063, which is before you, which -- this is the UNCIVPOL report for Sector South, and it reads -- or, rather, the date is 23 September 1992. You state that there was theft of wood in Kijevo and that victims were elderly Croats and that unknown suspects from Polaca cut and stole wood from the village. In your view, is this proof of the fact that the special police were persecuting Croats? You don't have to look at the Prosecutor. You can look either at the screen or at myself. I don't think the Prosecutor can help you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think -- I'm not quite sure what you mean by that, Mr. Milovancevic. But in any case your learned friend is on her feet. Yes, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Yes, just to point out that my learned friend refers to a specific page from this report but may be overlooking the fact that there are several reports that the statement, the witness statement, refers to, and then in the subsequent paragraph, he refers to trends from the reports in the plural. So I think it would be imprecise and incorrect to rely on one page from one report, wherever my learned friend is going on this point, to somehow suggest that this particular page refers to or is leading to a conclusion which refers to these reports in the plural.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not drawing any sort of conclusion. I was taking as a starting point the statement of this witness, which refers to this particular page as proof of fact that the special police were persecuting Croats. I wanted to know whether there was anything on this page, that's to say 7063, which constituted the basis for such a conclusion by the witness. I know that the report has 100 pages citing these cases. However, the Prosecution specifically referred you to these cases, and that's why I am following in their tracks and referring the witness to page 7063. And my question was whether this theft of wood was proof of the fact that the special police were intimidating Croats. And then I can draw your attention to another case dated 7 October 1992, death threats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you go to death threats, let the witness answer you on this one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could I look at the remaining ones, just in case?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, there was one there I would perhaps, if I had the page mentioned is one I would look at, with the hand-grenade thrown is a military item. This is the one there where is attempted murder, Marko, a hand-grenade was thrown into the house occupied by victims who was Knin milicija were contacted and no suspects. Again, if I have used the page I would suspect that that is the one that I drew on because of the fact that there was a hand-grenade involved. It's a military item.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does any element in this case enable you to arrive at the conclusion that the hand-grenade was hurled by the special police force? Secondly, do you see that there are Marko, Bozica and Natasa Juric cited here as victims, and that they were in an occupied house? Do you know what this means? Were they in their own house or in a home that they occupied that was someone else's in? And could this have been the reason for someone throwing a hand-grenade at them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do you mean they are in an occupied house? And where do you get that from?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is the event which took place on the 2nd of November, 1992 at Vrpolje which is S2-32/92. Victims are Marko, Bozica and Natasa Juric, and I was merely reading the text that's contained here, a hand-grenade was thrown into a house. This is the text we have here. Does the witness know whose house these persons occupied?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why do you ask these questions? You are saying they were in an occupied house. Occupied by whom and whose house is it? Because the text says a hand-grenade was thrown into a house occupied by the victims. Whether the house is an occupied house by somebody else, we don't know. But at the time it was occupied by the victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The gist of my question, Your Honour, was whether the witness allowed for the possibility that there was someone else other than the special police who had the motive to throw the hand-grenade at the house? And that was what my question aimed at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You didn't mention special police. You mentioned occupied house. Say what you mean then. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was quite specific. In paragraph 28, the witness states: "I have been shown a report dated 27 July, among others pages 7063." And then in paragraph 29 the witness says: "Trends from the reports I have been shown indicate that the special police were actively intimidating and expelling Croats." I can accept the reasoning whereby throwing a hand-grenade into someone's house constitutes intimidation, but on what basis did the victim come to the conclusion that this was perpetrated by the special police? This is what I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to clarify that, I just asked to go to the next one and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you clarify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Prosecutor is on her feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: I was just going to refer to the bottom entry on this page, Your Honours, which my learned colleague did not refer to in his questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Bottom entry, the one of the 5th of November, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't know whether he is still coming to that, but I'm still concerned with the one he was dealing with at the time, the one where the hand-grenade was thrown in. I see now Mr. Milovancevic is now telling us that he's referring us to paragraph 29. All I was asking him was why does he suggest that this house that was occupied by these victims did not belong to them, it was occupied by someone other person? Because that what he asked earlier. That's what I wanted to clear and that was never cleared and it has now disappeared. I can go back to the transcript, if we have to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise. I must have been following my reasoning. If you -- and I must have then disregarded what you were saying. When I saw the term "occupied," I thought that perhaps they were not in their own home but in someone else's home. I'm not sure whether such a possibility could have been inferred and that -- and that perhaps it was on this basis that the conclusion could have been drawn that this was the work of the special police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then let us read before we put questions so that we know exactly how the word "occupied" is used. And can I appeal to you to please not disregard what the Bench is saying to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, case 32/92, dated 2nd of November, 1992, involving a hand-grenade that was thrown into a house occupied by victims, do you have any information to the effect that the house belonged to the victims or perhaps that they were occupying someone else's house? Can any sort of conclusion along these lines be drawn on the basis of the text?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I would just like to add that at the outset I was referred to an incident of chopping wood or stealing wood, but when I stand down I saw another incident here of the last one, actually, 33/92, and I expect that that is the one I had selected when I made reference to the page. I had not seen it at the time because I was -- well, I suppose thrown a little bit by the fact that I had an incident referring to cutting wood placed as the basis for the issue. And it is that one I expect that I had selected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, when we are talking about this case, or rather the last case, involving Citluk and death threats, you can see that as victims, we have the following names listed here, Ana, Milka, Rajko, Ivan, Kata Knezevic. The short summary says that the Knin police told Croats to leave their houses or be killed and not to report that to CIVPOL. Do you distinguish between the special police and, let's say, the Knin police?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: They all came within the ambit of the police, but we knew that there was a division in the sense, and I mentioned it in my direct evidence, that we referred to what would be the regular police, so it is -- I've mentioned in general terms. It's mentioned in general terms, that is the Knin militia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does this report show whether you, as the civilian police, reported the incident to the Knin police and Mr. Martic to launch an investigation into the matter?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be normal practice for the district commander to raise issues of concern at local level, and, on occasions, issues that would come to headquarters would be raised by letter, and a number of those were documented and presented to the Court at an earlier stage. So it would be normal practice for the local district commander to follow through at that level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will refer you to two reports above this one, that's to say, the one dated 2nd November 1992, involving attempted murder, and the one above this one, the case dated 7 October 1992 involving death threats. In both cases, it was established that the Knin police had initiated an investigation and that even in the case of death threats it had offered protection, and in the other case that the Knin police were contacted but unfortunately no suspects were identified. You as a police officer of long standing, can you exclude the possibility that bandits and criminals can be found among the ranks of any police force in the world?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I would like to qualify that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Using the word "bandit" in the general sense, I suppose you'll find rogue individuals in any organisation and it is true in policing, but finding them in a large scale is perhaps a very unusual scenario.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As a -- indicator that points to the fact that members of the special police actively intimidated and prosecuted Croats, you also mentioned page 76 of the report that is before us. Can we see page 7066 and look at it to see what it says there? Can we have page 7066 on the screen, please? 7066. In the first case, the victim is Stipe Vujic and an unknown suspect shot at the house. Nobody was hurt. The Knin Milicija attended the scene. Is this evidence that the special police terrorised Croatian population in your view?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They did attend, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Interestingly enough, this person occupied somebody else's house, not his own. He was not in his own house. Therefore, somebody shot at it still. The next case, the victim is Katarina Maric. Somebody broke into her house and moved into it. The victim lives in Croatia. The house was abandoned, somebody broke into the house and moved in, the Knin police was contacted. Can this be treated as evidence that special police terrorised Croats?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The next case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry, sorry. I don't understand this to be saying that. It says a man and his family broke into a house and moved in. The house belongs to victim who now lives in Croatia. Okay. When does this victim -- does he live in Croatia after that -- after the break in or before the break in?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not clear from the report, Your Honour. I rushed into the conclusion, but you're absolutely right. I apologise. It says here the house belongs to victim who now lives in Croatia. Does it transpire from this that at the moment of the break in, the victim was in the house or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think common English would say "now" refers to the time of writing the report. Not common English but common sense. Isn't it at the time of writing the report? Because if it was at the time of the break in, it would have been "who then lived in Croatia" who then, at that time, of the break in, lived in Croatia. But if it is now lives in Croatia, we don't know whether he lives in Croatia because he has been chased out of his house or not. We -- an attempt --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The next act is theft marked as S217/93. The victim is Mirko Kovic, unknown suspects, stole 450 plants, and the police were contacted. Could this be another proof that the special police terrorised Croats?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The next report is relative to the 25th of January, 1993. We are familiar with the victim. He is a Croatian judge from Knin, Ivica Krvavica. He was mentioned by a previous witness who was -- victim -- witness who was here. He says in the report that four armed suspects were arrested by the Milicija after threatening to kill the victim. The suspects were later released, and the Milicija assured the victim that patrols would be made. Does this report speak about the special police threatening Croats?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The next report is relative to a crime against Anda Krvavica. It says that the victim was forced to leave her house by five uniformed men, to accommodate displaced Serbs. "In Potkonje, 30 Croats were forced out of their homes. These people were housed in a school and later they went to Croatia." Would this text provide you with an ability to conclude that the five uniformed men were the special police?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I ask you, Mr. Milovancevic, to please not read again what is there. Just point him to whatever you want to point him to and ask the question you want to ask. I think we are wasting a lot of time by you reading over and over again what is already there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. You're right. I understand. We are indeed wasting time. But sometimes I do this in order to explain why I'm putting my questions to the witness. With your leave, I would like to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The next case, the victim is Pera Gojevic. This happened on the 30th of January, 1993, and this is the last case on the page before us. The victim was found dead in a field and the Knin Milicija attended the scene. Which element from this report inspired you to conclude that the special police terrorised the Croats there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going back to the previous one, Your Honour. That is 20 of 93, where five uniformed men, the victim was force to leave her house by five uniformed men to accommodate displaced Serbs. That's the incident I have referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do you make of the fact that the Knin Milicija refused to investigate? In the next one, the one below.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, that would be a factor to be accounted as well and the fact that -- in that incident there was no cooperation. You can see in earlier ones there was. So, again, it's the variable that keeps emerging from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As regards your last answer, Mr. McElligott, do you recall that on the 22nd of January, 1993 - and the date here is the 30th of January, 1993 - the Croatian operation Maslenica was launched? I told you that 491 persons were killed during that operation. There were a lot of injured. All the UNCIVPOL stations had been evacuated to prevent casualties during the war operations. Would you allow for the possibility that the hospital did not have enough capacity to provide for the wounded let alone perform autopsies and that all the police officers were on the front line? I'm going to show you documents that talk about that. Will you allow for the possibility that this might have been the reason for this behaviour, rather than a lack of cooperation on the part of the Milicija who did not want to cooperate with the UNCIVPOL?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two issues there. One is the autopsy, and it says it was refused. There are no grounds given for that refusal. And then you have the total lack of cooperation with CIVPOL in the matter. And, again, I go back to the Vance Plan and the fact that everybody signed up to it. The least that one would expect in a situation, no matter how grave it was, that some liaison person would be left to link in with CIVPOL and at least keep a door open and show goodwill despite the circumstances, and I think I would regard it as not doing that as a serious issue. I would have expected at least a liaison person would be left available to maintain, to keep the door open. And this was in the headquarters in -- was it in Knin, was it? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We shall go back to that issue a bit later. As regards the previous case, involving people in the school, and that is one case up, one-but-last, are you aware of the fact that the monitors of the special police inspected the school?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Further on, when you say in paragraph 29, based on this, and on other pages of a similar nature, when you say that these are the basic indicators that the special police actively intimidated and prosecuted Croats, you say that the letter that was shown to you and that was signed by Martic indicates that he had command role over the special police unit and that he himself confirmed that there were no conditions for the safe return of the displaced Croats and that he himself would prevent them from returning if -- even if they wanted to return. Do you remember that in that letter Mr. Martic pointed to the problem of forceful return of the refugees that we have already mentioned today, and this forceful return of the Croatian refugees was something that the Croatian authorities tried to enforce? In his letter, Mr. Martic was pointing to the problem that might arise from such a procedure?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What's your question? Just ask one question, please, in one sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. McElligott, you say that you saw the letter signed by Martic, which in your view confirms that he himself says that there were no conditions in place for the return of the refugees, and that he himself would prevent the refugees from returning. My question was this: Do you know that Martic was trying -- is talking about an attempt to prevent the forceful return of the refugees that the Croatian authorities were trying to enforce, and are you aware of that, of the existence of that in the letter?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The letter does refer to returnees coming into the area, and he was pointing out that the environment was not correct at that time for that to take place. And the point I was making, based on the overall report, when you look at it in relation to the activity of the militia, that they were contributing to the environment that he was claiming was preventing them from coming. So that is the point I was making.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And the contribution of the special police that you saw, and the way you saw it, are all the cases that we saw on the previous page?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think when I make that comment, I make it on the basis of the overall report and information in addition to it, because we have to take into consideration accounts we have got from the community, who sleep in the forest by night and who have indicated the source of their problem, and they put it to the special police as the problem. So it wasn't based on a single block of this. The overall report and information in our possession and other factors taken into consideration would show that the special police were active in creating an environment that was not conducive to the return of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that people talked, and this is my last question today, did you verify any of those stories? Did the monitors check any of the stories that they had?

utterances.speaker: JOHN McELLIGOTT [Resumed]
utterances.text: They have met with people in the community. I met people myself who outlined their circumstances to me, and it was well-established with our monitors who went into the community; indeed, our monitors lived in the community, they lived in households with families and they were pretty well-established in communities. They got to know lots of people by travelling around, by meeting with them. So there was a good link with the community, and indeed, I think it could be said that the minority community, the Croatian element of it, would have regarded them as their police force rather than anybody else, and I think that was based on fears of what would happen in relation to the police in existence in the sector. So there was a lot of feedback coming from what was going on in communities, and it was not complimentary to the local police. And I think anybody who would sleep in the wood in the middle of winter would be quite frank in disclosing the source of the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think the moment has come for me to wrap it up for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. We will convene tomorrow at what time? 2.00? 2.00 in the afternoon. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: be reconvened on Tuesday, the 30th day of May, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.
